body:
# Mūt — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Mūt, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Mūt to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𐤌𐤕**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Mūt**.

And the marks themselves: **o → ū** (Macron: long /uː/ (Mūt)). Remove any one of them and you have not simplified the name — you have told a small lie about it, and small lies in references have long consequences.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'MOHT' — one syllable with a long, drawn-out o (or oo) and a crisp final t. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *mot* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *mot* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible. Every mark it drops — *o → ū* — is a fact the sources recorded. A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

Now to the forms that provoked your letter. As for *Mut*: it comes from the publisher compromise — older books and hurried websites that print the "English equivalent" as if it were the name itself, and it fails because every substitution here (ū→u) is a romanization of convenience, not an attested spelling — it teaches the reader to guess, not to read As for *Mút*: it comes from the near-miss — a form that looks right at a glance and circulates on wikis and forums, and it fails because a macron marks length; an acute marks tone — different facts

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The Hellenistic Phoenician account preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea — quoting Philo of Byblos, who summarized Sanchuniathon — makes Mōt (Muth) a son of El and Rhea, deified after death and identified by the Phoenicians with the Greek Thanatos and Pluto.  A more speculative cosmogonic strand in the same tradition makes Mōt arise from primal mud or putrefaction, the source from which the seeds of creation emerge.

And it never stopped working. Mōt's name survives in Hebrew māwet, Arabic mawt, and the Semitic root for death itself.  His myth helped shape later personifications of death in biblical and apocalyptic literature, and the Baꜥal-Mōt cycle has long fascinated scholars of ancient religion as a Near Eastern parallel to — and a warning against facile equations with — later dying-and-rising god traditions.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Mūt** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *mot* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Mūt** stands at [/mot/](/mot/).

The docket for this ruling: 2 false forms ruled against, *Mut* first on the docket; 1 preserved mark verified: **o → ū**; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 9 cited sources — KTU (Ugaritic texts), Smith, The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Coogan, Stories from Ancient Canaan.
